newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris shows bounce from jasmine to hydrangea.
newsitem.headline: Paris shows bounce from jasmine to hydrangea.

text.p: Chiffons in shades of a sunset over Bora-Bora or the waters of a Tahitian lagoon swirled down the catwalk at French designer Rosette Torrente-Mette's summery haute couture collection on Sunday.
A statuesque woman performing Polynesian dance and "natives" handing out jasmine flowers to the fashion crowd set the stage for this feminine collection gleaned from exotic island flora and fauna.
There were plenty of ostrich-skin coats in beige, dusty rose and lime, orange suede dresses and tunics embroidered with eyelet lace, and canary-coloured hide trousers.
From the demure Jackie Kennedy suits of lacquered irridescent brocade to the New Look crinoline petticoats, it was gay and ladylike, if short on modernity and innovation.

"I would say it was a superb collection which has the advantage of being wearable. Rosette Mette understands perfectly the needs of an active woman," smiled former French Socialist Prime Minister Edith Cresson.
"It was a glamorous collection but for myself I prefer no colour. I like black, beige," said the actress clad in black.
"But it is a summer collection, so I suppose the pastels were right. I do like to wear them on the beach."
French couturiers have been desperately searching for themes to give their collections focus to counter a dwindling customer base and the increasing prominence of foreign designers.

The day was dominated by suspense over irreverent Briton Alexander McQueen's first collection for Givenchy and ready-to-wear star Jean-Paul Gaultier's first-ever couture show, both scheduled later on Sunday.
Meanwhile, the fashion set sat impatiently through other shows.
Frenchman Olivier Lapidus gleaned inspiration from Mother Nature herself, composing an "ecological premiere...joining luxury and agricultural products".

Lapidus said he had crafted the clothes from vegetable fibres, creating such textiles as "doupion based on mint, satin organdies mixed with blackcurrant, silk jersey and daisies, grapevine leaves or raspberry".
Rose petals covered the catwalk and nestled in the models' hair-dos.

But aside from the hydrangea-petal cuffs and collar of a lichen-green jacket, or the moss ruff at the neckline of a natty bolero, Nature's utility most often went no further than inspiring Lapidus's floral prints: a daffodil-strewn jumpsuit or the roses spreading across a satin dustcoat with matching hot-pants.
